# Original 2014 Cicada Freenode log corpus: recovered public source locator

**Agent40, 14 November 2026. Independently recovered period-origin community record, not a Cicada-authored cipher instruction.** The previous research frontier treated the original May–August 2014 `#cicadasolvers` Freenode transcripts as absent. An existing public fork of the original `neuroretransmit/cicada` archive contains two full `#cicadasolvers` channel logs, with **236,650 timestamped 2014 lines in the first file**, and an additional 38,008 from September–December in the second. A separate `#33012014` channel file has a further 110,607 timestamped 2014 lines. All three original files were fully retrieved and verified byte-for-byte against original Git blob identifiers on GitHub Actions. The exact original chat records are accessible as complete Git objects, with timestamps and participant-attributed text; they are not an interpretation assembled from modern walkthroughs.

## Original source file identities and coverage

The public source is [the preserved IRC log directory](https://github.com/cicada-solvers/neuroretransmit-cicada/tree/main/irc-logs), retaining filenames of the older original `neuroretransmit/cicada` tree. The three pinned original source objects are:

| [`#cicadasolvers.freenode.2.log`](https://github.com/cicada-solvers/neuroretransmit-cicada/blob/main/irc-logs/%23cicadasolvers.freenode.2.log) | 27,234,234 | `72634a9d071d32af767edbffc0493d810e88cd0d` | September–December 2014: 38,008 dated lines; also 2015–16 |

The full `#cicadasolvers` first-file 2014 monthly counts (source text lines prefixed `2014 Mon DD HH:MM`) are **Jan 94,818; Feb 43,172; Mar 15,101; Apr 8,901; May 29,249; Jun 23,228; Jul 13,836; Aug 8,235; Sep 110**. This proves **74,548 directly dated May–August 2014 channel lines** in the original primary channel file. The separate #33012014 source adds another **2,091** dated May–August 2014 lines. Exact original timestamps are recorded with minute resolution; these are date-bearing text exports and not cryptographic proof of the identities behind nicknames.

Some May–August original channel posts specifically mention `http://titanpad.com/vFCy7T5p0O` and a separate transcription pad `http://titanpad.com/hJ8pVQ5S43`. **Update, 15 November 2026:** the latter pad's *original editable document* has not been recovered, but an explicitly pad-attributed transcription survives as two dateable 2015 Git blobs in [`resvolver/c1cada`](https://github.com/resvolver/c1cada/commit/42d33941f0f03223c01fe052c0ae91a7a4981eb5) and its January-23 correction. The corrected 2015 derivative matches 47/57 original rune-bearing pages exactly and differs by 70 edit operations on the other ten, including a wrong rune on solved p56. This is a historical source witness, not a newly authenticated puzzle key. See [the precise page comparison and scope](../../im-results/2015-hj8pvq5s43-pad-derived-transcription.md). On **19 August 2014 23:56**, `#cicadasolvers` has a line stating that someone asked about the page-56 hash on StackExchange. These are historical participant observations, not a solved preimage or an original author response. The source also contains IRC messages under nickname `cluosh` before and during 2014, the name credited with the original p56 solution; no independent identity attestation follows from the nickname. **First historical p56 solve, 19 May 2014, recovered in the original log.** The primary channel supplies a complete first-person sequence under the IRC nickname `cluosh`:
- **01:55–01:56, source L180878–87:** mentions the prime sequence from the May-2 upload, explicitly includes missing **19**, and announces `AN END: WITHIN` for page 56.
- **01:58, L180896–906:** identifies primes modulo 29 as GP29 shifting values, extending plaintext to `AN END: WITHIN THE`.
- **02:09–02:18, L180931–64:** rejects a mistakenly inferred 19-symbol repeating key, publishes consecutive prime-minus-one residues (`1-2-4-6-10-12-16-18-22-28...`) and specifies `ciphertext - key = clear`.
- **02:30–02:35, L181015–48:** another participant (`mdzhb`) prints the complete non-hash English message and identifies the book's first successful page solve.
- **02:51–03:01, L181096–131:** `cluosh` says `AN END` was already a guessed plaintext crib; the group identifies the unencrypted plaintext `F` and the no-key-advance rule.
- **21 May, L184921–28:** `cluosh` says that guessing the first two words enabled the prime interpretation, acknowledges possible luck, and explains that the Euler-totient description came later.

This clarifies the May-15 `totient` question (L178827) immediately followed by `jk` (L178828), which **does not** date a successful solve; June-19 L205898/L206244 are much later retellings. The original upload's visible whitespace run counts 2,3,5,7,11,13,17,23,29,31,37 fit the reported missing-19 prime sequence, **but ten of those runs are not signed** and archived copies differ at 7/23 versus 6/22. Thus the IRC evidence establishes the human solver's selection path without authenticating the upload's incidental bytes as a reusable LP2 key. This source first-method extraction was verified against all original log blobs in [successful CI 43603578484](https://github.com/FlareZ123/liber-primus/actions/runs/43603578484), using [the CommonJS exact-byte SFT](../../sims/lp2_2014_p56_method_origin_sft.cjs). p56 complete authenticity is separately verified in [the existing regression](../../im-results/authentic-decryption-regression.md). The direct 11-value upload prime reuse on p0 already failed in [the bounded original-cipher test](../../im-results/historical-may2-whitespace-source-gate.md); no unknown-page plaintext is inferred.

**2014 unknown-page crib witness screen:** A second source-identical, cross-message [dialogue and key-claim screen](../../sims/lp2_2014_irc_inchannel_dialogue_sft.cjs) found a **23 May 2014 L186651** speculation that p54 starts `A Beginning`, explicitly qualified `beginning doesn't fit`; this predates the archived May **2016** Titanpad iteration of that crib. The same original dialogue gives a **16 May 2014 L179463–64** participant-suggested formula `M(n)=abs(3301-P(F(n)+1))`. This is **exactly the known generator of the original p15 Fibonacci-prime 4×4 square**, reproducing all 16 cells under the unique-Fibonacci clockwise center-out order ([existing exact artifact SFT](../../sims/fibonacci_prime_spiral.cjs)). It is a source-dated recognition of an authentic printed-math operation, **without a specified ciphertext-to-plaintext GP29 inverse, unknown-page plaintext or key**. [Original-byte Windows CI 43611424980](https://github.com/FlareZ123/liber-primus/actions/runs/43611424980).  The same first-party source record also preserves hypothetical non-p56 plaintext guesses on May21 p25 (`CONDITIONEDNESS`), May24 p35 (`IT'S` with shifts 26–28) and p34 (`LESS` with shifts 27,28,0,1), and May27 p11 (`OVERSIMPLIFYING`). These are explicitly tentative guesses and the original phase progression **fails immediately** on the untouched next p34 and p35 printed words (`EFE` and `JSDD`). The 2014 participants had no reproducible broader page solution in those captured contexts. [Source-pinned full witness screen and original-rune holdout](../../im-results/lp2-2014-original-irc-unknown-page-crib-holdout.md) · [successful CI run 43606051226](https://github.com/FlareZ123/liber-primus/actions/runs/43606051226).


## Original 2014 p49–51 numeric-table discussion and proposed cipher families

The pinned primary `#cicadasolvers.freenode.log` object above also preserves the original human solve path around the new LP2 table. These are **participant observations and hypotheses**, not signed Cicada instructions:

| Date and original log lines | What participants actually said or tried | Evidentiary status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 May, L166285–309; L166749–820 | They identify pages 49–51, first ask whether the numbers are base64, then discuss a 256-byte object. `f10ur1ick3r` links Babylonian numerals/sexagesimal and says the field is base60; `lvkm` says each two-character pair is one number/byte. The same conversation notices the recurring cuneiform values 17, 13, 55, 1 on pp33–39. | Period-origin human interpretation of the printed field; it is not an author-specified decoder for the rune text. |
| 6 May, L168995–999 | `f10ur1ick3r` reports narrowing RSA `e,d` to 52 possible pairs and proposes that RSA applied to the 256-byte base60 field may yield the key for the 128-byte hex field near the end of the book. | A contemporaneous RSA hypothesis, not a recovered private key, verified plaintext, or successful result. |
| 7 May, L170978–983 | `Ammar__` conjectures that both a word's GP value and rune position may enter the prime value or the index of the key/cipher rune, and reports an unexplained relation between a cipher-rune prime and plaintext-word GP. L170981 separately connects cuneiform to 1033/3301 in base60 and says illustrations may matter. | An unusually relevant early word-value × rune-position hypothesis, explicitly unproved by its author. The adjacent claim that only p56 matters is another participant's opinion, not consensus. |
| 13 May, L177314–329; 14 May, L177734–740 and L178383–404 | Participants note 256 base60 values alongside three earlier 256-hex strings, say that combinations/XOR had not produced a result, and discuss XORing page images. On 14 May one asks about fitting the p49–51 base60 string into a biliteral matrix; another suggests self-synchronizing stream ciphers. No successful decode or follow-up is recorded in this context. | Exploratory community suggestions and documented failures; neither suggestion is a Cicada-authored selector. |

**Current research disposition.** The repository has already tested several concrete descendants of the biliteral suggestion: the original 32×64 bitplane/printed-order and one-bit parity view ([`lp2-grid-bitplane-order.md`](../../im-results/lp2-grid-bitplane-order.md)) and source-visible case-bitplanes, including a five-bit Bacon-style readout and AES-256 consumers ([`lp2-p50-case-bitplane-aes256-source-gate.md`](../../im-results/lp2-p50-case-bitplane-aes256-source-gate.md)). These do not prove that every imaginable A/B classification is impossible; the 2014 log itself supplies no selected threshold, digit position, grouping or reading direction, so further bitplane sweeps would be unconstrained. Likewise, the log's RSA and self-synchronizing-stream suggestions are hypotheses, not permission to tune keys, nonces or modes without an independent selector.

The May-7 word-GP/rune-position idea is a period-origin precedent for testing joint word/rune state, but it remains a participant conjecture. It is relevant context for the current word-number/pointer investigation; do not upgrade it to author intent or a verified mechanism. The original source object is still the same pinned 18,487,233-byte blob `bdd277c14f94c34b5ae714cd00c238065beeed4e`; line numbers above refer to that exact object.


## Original 2014 p54 red-title guesses and the recovered modcipher attempt

The same original channel records a later, distinct p54-title discussion on **2 July 2014**, lines **216910–931**. `Anoniem4l` says the second red word after the large `A` is **not DIRECTION**, then tests the eight-rune guess `D-I-R-E-C-T-IO-N`; `f10ur1ick3r` suggests `deception` or `beginnings`, and the participants discuss `Beginning` versus `beginnings`. The original p54 scan (archive image `71.jpg`) prints `A-M-NG-D-IA-TH-X-I-M`: the red word after A has exactly eight canonical GP29 runes, `M, NG, D, IA, TH, X, I, M`.

The 2014 p56 decoder explicitly records the aliases `IA/IO` and `NG/ING`; the corpus uses `IA` and `NG` as canonical spellings. **DIRECTION** → `D-I-R-E-C-T-IO-N` and **DECEPTION** → `D-E-C-E-P-T-IO-N` each fit eight runes through the `IO` alias. **BEGINNING** also has an eight-rune spelling, `B-E-G-I-N-N-I-NG`, when the final `I` and `NG` are separate symbols; the alternate `ING)-as-one-rune spelling gives only seven. Thus all three have an eight-rune reading, but BEGINNING's fit depends on the chosen transliteration segmentation. The 2014 participant's rejection of DIRECTION and claim that BEGINNING was too short are solver judgments, not decisive length tests. The source does not select among the candidates, and none is decrypted.

The recovered participant script `2014-irc-shared/anoniem4l-modcracker-M5BccDpT.py` has `our = [71,79,89,107,5,47,31,71]`, exactly the ordinal-prime values of the eight observed p54 red-title runes. Its eight-entry `want` array `[89,31,11,63,13,59,107,29]` is commented as `D-I-R-E-C-T-IO-N`; the `IO` alias is valid, but its E value 63 differs from the canonical ordinal-prime value 67. The script also has a defective final predicate: it compares the first two candidate differences but only truth-tests the remaining six, rather than requiring all eight to be equal. A corrected all-eight constant-modulus-shift test over every modulus 1–330 finds **no modulus** for canonical DIRECTION prime values `[89,31,11,67,13,59,107,29]`, DECEPTION `[89,67,13,67,43,59,107,29]`, or the eight-symbol BEGINNING spelling `[61,67,17,31,29,29,31,79]`. The alternate seven-symbol BEGINNING spelling cannot match the eight-rune ciphertext. This rejects that simple modcipher consumer for the length-compatible candidates; it does not test or reject the separate p56 red-title key schedule.

These are contemporary solver cribs and experiments, not Cicada-signed plaintext or author instructions. The 23 May 2014 `A Beginning` guess and 2 July discussion are independent historical occurrences; the length-compatible spellings do not establish which, if any, is plaintext.

## Reproduction and research significance

[The original-byte CommonJS SFT](../../sims/lp2_2014_original_irc_log_source_gate_sft.cjs) checks every Git blob SHA1 and exact original byte count before computing per-year/per-month tallies and extracting source-line numbers for p56/hash/totality clues. [Successful original-source GitHub Actions run 43599552893](https://github.com/FlareZ123/liber-primus/actions/runs/43599552893) recovered all three complete files, verified them, and printed source line numbers and counts. Existing earlier [May-2014-pad archival research](../../im-results/lp2-2014-may-unfiction-workpad-source-gate.md) had found only April–July **2016** snapshots and no 2014 chat; the present original IRC discovery materially resolves that historical acquisition gap, independently of recovering any original target URL.

This public source may enable historically grounded testing of when p56 was first decoded, which keys were proposed, and whether anyone recorded the unidentified continuation URL. It must be inspected for actual messages before crediting any claim. Nicknames, channel URLs, participant guesses and records from `#33012014` should remain distinct from signed Cicada instructions. **No unsolved original LP2 plaintext, matching p56 digest preimage, or historical intended key has been recovered by this discovery alone.**
